cards.title: Build and grow an engaged subscriber segment
cards.summary: Define an engaged audience using email and on-site behaviors, then expand reach by slowly re-introducing dormant subscribers in random chunks.
cards.use_when: You are planning a retention or email marketing operation and need to decide who to send to, or you want to grow reachable subscribers ahead of a major sale.
steps: Define an engaged audience as people who opened or clicked an email OR took on-site actions like add-to-cart, started checkout, or placed an order within a lookback window.

Set lookback windows that reflect your lifecycle and repurchase cadence (the source example used ~180 days for opens/clicks, ~220 days for other actions, and ~280 days for orders — treat these as source-specific heuristics, not fixed rules).
Build the segment in your ESP (e.g., Klaviyo) and note its current size as your base sendable audience.
Split the remaining unengaged/dormant portion into random samples (the source used 10 samples of equal size) so you can add them back in controlled batches.
Add one sample to an engaged send at a time, sending your best content, and measure how many newly open or engage, then fold them into the engaged segment.
Repeat this in batches over several months, measuring the engaged segment size as your key retention KPI and aiming for it to grow over time.
Reserve dormant-reactivation pushes for marketing calendar peaks (e.g., Black Friday) when strong offers are most likely to convert them.
caveats: Opening/engagement assumptions (e.g., 20–30% open rates) are illustrative from the source, not guaranteed benchmarks.
The source's Black Friday +40% YoY result is a single brand example, not a promise.
Assumes your ESP supports behavioral segmentation and random sampling.

cards.title: Use flows for personalization, campaigns for reach
cards.summary: Reserve behavior-triggered flows for one-to-one personalization and use broader campaigns for reach and brand moments.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how to allocate effort between automated flows and broadcast campaigns, or where to apply personalization in your email/SMS program.
steps: Route personalization to flows: triggers fire on specific behaviors (purchase, abandoned checkout, browse) where you have real data to act on.
Within flows, first split by customer journey stage, then layer product or collection splits for finer personalization.
Route reach and brand moments to campaigns: use broader messaging, educational and entertaining content to reach as many subscribers as possible.
Recognize only a small share of your list (the source cites ~3%) is ready to buy today; broad campaigns appeal to the ~97% not ready to buy but still willing to engage.
Measure campaign success by engagement and reach growth, and flow success by behavior-driven conversion.
Avoid micro-niche campaign segmentation; reserve segmented sends for specific goals (e.g., VIP revenue) within a roughly 80% reach / 20% specific-goal split.
caveats: The 80/20 reach split is the source's recommended heuristic, not a universal rule.
The ~3% ready-to-buy figure is an illustrative estimate.

cards.title: Define VIPs by revenue and profit share
cards.summary: Identify VIPs as the segment driving roughly 50%+ of revenue and ~80% of profit, then decide whether to invest in them based on your actual constraint.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to build VIP campaigns, a loyalty program, or VIP flow pathways, or deciding whether first-to-second order conversion should take priority.
steps: Define VIPs by revenue share: the source treats customers driving ~50%+ of revenue and ~80% of profit as the VIP segment because they return more often and rely less on discounts.
Validate this against your own data before rewarding — the 50/80 split is source-specific guidance, not a universal benchmark.

Before building VIP programming, identify your actual constraint: if VIP revenue and profit shares are already healthy and you struggle with first-to-second order conversion, prioritize that constraint first.

If VIP revenue is your constraint, use segmented campaigns (part of the ~20% specific-goal split) to drive VIP value via exclusive products, sales, early access, offline events/community, and loyalty/perk reminders.
Bake VIP pathways into flows: dedicated VIP perks and loyalty-focused branches rather than treating VIPs identically to everyone else.
The source suggests VIP programs become higher leverage for brands above roughly $10–20M annual revenue; below that, first-to-second order conversion is often the bigger constraint.
caveats: The $10–20M revenue threshold and 50%/80% split are the source's heuristics, not established calculations.
Only pursue VIP incrementality when it is actually your constraint; otherwise it is low-leverage.

cards.title: Run RFM analysis to segment on real purchase behavior
cards.summary: Score subscribers on Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value relative to your own customer base to build actionable cohorts.
cards.use_when: You are building customer segments for win-back flows, replenishment, VIP campaigns, or first-to-second order conversion.
steps: Use RFM scoring: score each subscriber on how recently they purchased, how frequently they purchase, and how much they spend — all relative to your own subscriber base, not external benchmarks.

Classify subscribers into segments: Champions (top percentiles across all three), Loyal (just below Champions), Recent (recent purchase but not frequent/high-spend), At Risk (metrics slowing), and Needs Attention.
Treat At Risk and Needs Attention similarly in practice: get in front of them to prompt a purchase, especially if they were previously a Champion.
Build a high-value win-back segment of former Champions who are now At Risk or Needs Attention, and target them in the ~20% specific-goal campaigns.
Replace arbitrary win-back triggers (e.g., 120 days) with RFM-driven triggers so a 200-day-cycle high-spender isn't sent a generic discount prematurely.
Use RFM segments across flows (win-back, replenishment, post-purchase, abandoned cart/checkout) where you can trigger off real behavioral data.
Target Recent-but-not-Loyal/Champion customers as a first-to-second order conversion segment to elevate them before they lapse.
Set up RFM in your platform's analytics tab (e.g., Klaviyo marketing analytics) or wherever your software supports it, and verify current interface.
caveats: RFM scores are relative to your own base, so definitions shift as your customer mix changes.
The cohort labels are the source's framework; exact percentile cutoffs aren't fixed.

cards.title: Use paid ads to surface new arrivals to existing customers
cards.summary: For fashion and drop-driven brands, allocate dedicated paid spend to existing customers to surface new products, measured against tighter efficiency KPIs.
cards.use_when: You run frequent product drops or new arrivals and need to decide whether to spend paid media against your existing customer base.
steps: Recognize paid ads is primarily an acquisition tool; the source's default position is to spend little on existing customers — verify this fits your model before reallocating.

Exception: in fashion and continuously-dropping categories, paid ads are needed to surface new arrivals because email/SMS alone won't reach the whole existing base and new products shouldn't be missed.
Run a dedicated existing-customer spend surfacing new arrivals and current campaign shoots.

Set tighter KPI targets for existing-customer campaigns: if your new-customer CPA target is e.g. $40, the source suggests targeting $20 or lower for existing customers due to warm-audience efficiency.

Watch for diminishing returns: beyond a point, more spend on a small existing base doesn't drive more conversions, so pull back spend while maintaining conversion volume and reallocate the savings to acquisition.
Instead of a percentage allocation, compute a dollar budget: frequency (source suggests 4–7 per month) × number of existing customers × CPMs ÷ 1,000.
caveats: The source notes it was previously wrong to say never spend on existing customers — this is a situational exception.
The $20 CPA and 4–7 frequency figures are source heuristics, not fixed rules.
Requires your measurement setup to isolate incremental existing-customer conversions.

cards.title: Audit discount-acquired cohorts for LTV quality
cards.summary: Acquire customers on discount only after checking whether those cohorts have worse repeat rates, which the source says affects a majority of brands.
cards.use_when: You are planning promotions or discount-driven acquisition (e.g., BFCM) and deciding whether the front-end performance reflects true customer value.
steps: Treat acquisition discounting as a hypothesis to test, not a default: during discount periods front-end metrics (ROAS, efficiency, new-customer volume) look better, but that can be misleading.
Run a cohort analysis breaking customers down by discount code taken and measure lifetime value and repeat purchase rate for each cohort.

The source's generalization: for roughly 60% of brands they work with, discount-acquired customers have substantially worse LTV — but this does not apply to all brands (the source cites some 9-figure retailers where it doesn't), so pull your own numbers.
Investigate cause: discounts open you to a wider, price-motivated demographic that doesn't repeat buy once prices return to normal.
Adjust acquisition strategy based on findings — if discounted cohorts are worse, weigh the front-end lift against long-term quality before scaling the offer.
caveats: The ~60% figure is the source's generalization across its client base, not a universal rule.
Some large retailers see no LTV penalty from discount acquisition.
Cohort quality takes time to measure; don't overreact to early signals.

cards.title: Use zero-party data to improve acquisition targeting
cards.summary: Collect zero-party data (customer preferences, problems, motivations) to define personas and angles, then feed top- and bottom-customer insights back into paid ads.
cards.use_when: You are designing acquisition creative, personas, or angles, or setting up post-purchase surveys to inform paid media.
steps: Distinguish first-party data (email, phone, name) from zero-party data (personal info shared by the customer): what they do on weekends, what problem the product solves, what they like about the brand.
Collect zero-party data via surveys (post-purchase surveys mentioned as a method) and store it tied to customer records.
Analyze the top 20% of customers (which the source says typically drive 80% of revenue): identify their persona, the angles they responded to, and the offer they purchased on.
Force those top-20% patterns into paid ads and overallocate spend toward them to acquire more lookalike customers.

Analyze the bottom 20% of customers: identify their personas, angles, and offers — often these came in on an angle misaligned with the product (e.g., a skin-health supplement acquired on an 'energy' angle), causing returns, refunds, and no repurchase.
Exclude or reduce front-end spend on misaligned angles even if they show strong front-end ROAS, because the mismatch produces low-quality customers.
caveats: The 20/80 revenue split is the source's stated typical pattern, not a fixed rule.
Misaligned-angle detection often only surfaces through customer support feedback or surveys, so set up a capture mechanism.
Persona and angle insights require connecting post-purchase survey data to ad performance data.

cards.title: Measure engaged-segment growth as your core retention KPI
cards.summary: Track the size of your engaged audience over time as the primary email retention metric, rather than optimizing each broadcast in isolation.
cards.use_when: You are setting retention KPIs, reviewing email/SMS performance, or deciding whether a reactivation strategy is working.
steps: Make the primary retention KPI the size of your engaged segment and whether it grows over time, not just per-campaign open or click rates.
Recompute the engaged segment on a consistent lookback window (source examples: ~180/220/280 days) so growth is comparable period to period.
When adding dormant subscribers back into sends, measure how many convert from unengaged to engaged and roll them into the engaged segment to capture net growth.
Use marketing calendar peaks to accelerate engaged growth: push strong offers to re-engaged subscribers when conversion is most likely.
Review engaged-segment growth over months (source cites 6–9 month windows) rather than week to week, and adjust sampling batch sizes accordingly.
Pair segment-growth tracking with broader retention metrics (repeat rate, VIP revenue share) to ensure growth is producing revenue, not just opens.
caveats: Engagement definitions and lookback windows are source-specific; adapt to your lifecycle.
Open rates are increasingly unreliable as an engagement signal; on-site actions like add-to-cart and checkout starts strengthen the definition.
The source's +40% YoY BFCM result is an anecdote, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Reward VIPs with exclusivity rather than broad discounts
cards.summary: Give VIPs exclusive products, early access, perks, and experiences instead of treating them like the general list.
cards.use_when: You are designing VIP campaigns, a loyalty program, or flow pathways and want to increase VIP revenue without cheapening the relationship.
steps: Identify your VIP segment (revenue/profit leaders) and separate it from the general list in both campaign and flow builds.
Offer exclusivity rather than discounts: the source cites exclusive products, private sales, early access, offline experiences, and community/event perks as effective VIP rewards.
Use VIP campaigns for reminders about loyalty-program perks and benefits already attached to their account, since VIPs may not track these.
Build VIP branches into automated flows (VIP pathways) so the perks and treatment are consistent beyond campaigns.
Follow the 80% reach / 20% specific-goal campaign split, using VIP-focused campaigns as the more targeted 20% when driving VIP revenue is a goal.
Only invest in VIP programs when VIP revenue is your actual constraint; otherwise prioritize other constraints such as first-to-second order conversion first.
caveats: VIP rewards should not simply mirror general-list tactics; the source advises against treating VIPs like everyone else.
The source cautions against chasing VIP incrementality when your real constraint lies elsewhere.
